extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / early-18th-century literate public interested in taste, theatre, and manners
extracted.subtask_description: Essayistic prescriptions and critiques about humor, theatrical performance, literary taste, and public manners (early 18th-century). Includes standards for writing, acting, and what pleases a refined audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and relevance in anecdote/repartee
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid being so very circumstantial and careful to be exact that one 'plays away its Words, with uttering nothing to the Purpose.' Do not settle irrelevant geography or extraneous detail in a jest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep stories and repartees concise and directed to the point; do not delay the jest with needless parentage, locations, or proofs that add nothing to the humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive appeal to authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not bolster a simple point by piling on learned citations (e.g. naming multiple divines, sermon numbers and page references) when the matter needs no such authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust one's own parts and judgment rather than overloading an argument or comic point with pompous references; excessive reading-out of authorities signals humility misplaced and diminishes effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject pedantry and frivolous disputation
rubrics_metrics.description: One ought not to turn small matters into labored arguments or raise perpetual doubts (e.g. putting people to prove obvious facts or denying the existence of colour), thereby becoming 'always frivolous and always unanswerable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the habit of cavilling, hair-splitting, or disputing trivialities — it makes wit barren and audience patience thin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise, graceful theatrical speaking — small faults intolerable
rubrics_metrics.description: In theatrical speaking, if the performer is not exactly proper and graceful, he is utterly ridiculous; 'the least Diminution of that Pleasure is the highest Offence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors must aim for exactness and grace in delivery; slight awkwardness that diminishes auditory or visual pleasure is unacceptable on the legitimate stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep corporeal/acrobatic feats off the legitimate stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporeal and intellectual actors ought to be kept at a wider distance; rope-dancers and tumblers (physical feats) entertain a different faculty and belong to the bear-garden rather than the serious theatre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve dangerous or spectacle-driven bodily stunts for venues catering to that taste; do not conflate acrobatics with the dramatic art aimed at refined audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject-matter to genre — avoid tragic devices in comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects like witchcraft and dark, horrid ceremonies (effective in Macbeth/Tragedy) are 'extremely foreign from the Affair of Comedy' and cannot be rendered entertaining in comedy except by a genius like Shakespeare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose comic subjects appropriate to comedy's aims; do not transplant horror/tragic machinery into comic works unless you possess extraordinary imaginative power to transform them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indecent or libertine jests that offend modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of some passages that raise loud mirth may nevertheless be 'painful to right Sense, and an Outrage upon Modesty' and sacrifice the best part of the audience to the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pander to the lowest tastes with coarse jests; protect modesty and the sensibilities of the more discerning audience members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral responsibility in dramatic resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conclude plays with facile moral evasions (e.g. 'There is a Fate which over-rules us still') that excuse immoral actions such as marrying without consent; such endings can sanitize wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights should avoid framing immoral conduct as inevitable or excusable by fate; endings should not undermine virtuous standards or teach bad examples by casual gloss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to please people of best understanding, not merely the lowest appetites
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should raise their genius to please 'People of the best Understanding' and not write chiefly to gratify those who only seek risibility; otherwise they 'sacrifice the best Part of his Audience to the worst.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with the tastes of a refined, discerning audience in mind; do not tailor work solely to popular coarse amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary taste: prefer the just, proper, and natural over affected wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitators who value uncouth or antique words, forced antithesis, or 'point' and 'turn' over what is just, proper and natural are misguided; 'what is Just, Proper and Natural does not seem to be the Question' for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek naturalness and propriety in language and thought; avoid quaint antitheses, forced allusions, and superficial imitation of mannerisms (e.g. Miltonic uncouthness or Cowleyesque turns) as substitutes for true wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of glory (criteria for public greatness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tully's perfection of glory consists in these three particulars: 'That the People love us; that they have Confidence in us; that being affected with a certain Admiration towards us, they think we deserve Honour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a ruler's glory, distinguish durable, virtuous fame (rooted in public love, confidence, and deserved admiration) from empty ostentation; under monarchical contexts add dependence on the prince's favour as a necessary component for certain forms of 'glory.'

rubrics_metrics.name: True gallantry in love: Christian, honourable, and modest expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: True gallantry consists in solid, long-lasting regard grounded in virtue, good breeding, education, piety, and mutual esteem — not in 'Romantick Hero' or 'Whining Coxcomb' affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor expressions of love that show constancy, modesty, piety, and mutual improvement; reject theatrical or affected courtship that prizes show over steady worth.
